Verified — but weaker than I first read it. `onDidMutate` already force-refreshes workroom status, so the on-screen divergence window is sub-second, not 15s. Downgrading that to a DRY finding rather than a bug, and stating it with a caveat.

**`[P2] (confidence: 8/10)` — `VCSRemoteState` and `VCSSyncSnapshot` are two structs mirroring ~8 of the same fields.**

The engine returns `VCSRemoteState { current, tracking, refs, remotes, primaryRemote, lastFetch, … }`. The presentation mapper takes `VCSSyncSnapshot { branch, hasRemote, upstream, ahead, behind, lastFetch, pullRebase, activity, failure, lastAction }`. Branch, remote presence, upstream, both counts and `lastFetch` all appear twice, with a hand-written translation between them that nothing else needs.

questions.question:
D8 — Collapse the two overlapping state structs into one? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-cq-dry-2>

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. Plan defines `VCSRemoteState` (engine output) and `VCSSyncSnapshot` (mapper input) with ~8 duplicated fields.

ELI10: The plan has the engine produce one description of the repo's remote state, then hand-copies most of it into a second, differently-shaped struct just so the presentation function can read it. Every field that exists in both places is a field two types have to agree about, and a translation step that can silently drop or mistranslate one. The second struct earns its keep for exactly three things the first doesn't carry: whether a workroom is even selected, whether it's a repo at all, and the repo's pull-rebase setting.

Stakes if we pick wrong: keeping both means every new piece of remote state gets added in two places plus the mapping between them, and the translation is untested surface sitting between two tested layers. Collapsing wrongly means the pure, easily-testable mapper starts depending on a bigger engine type and gets harder to construct in tests.

Recommendation: A — one struct, with the three presentation-only facts as parameters to the mapper rather than mirrored fields. The mapper stays pure and the duplication goes away. Directly maps to your "flag repetition aggressively" preference.

✅ Confines the translation to one initializer that can itself be unit-tested, rather than scattering field copies at call sites.

ELI10: The plan has the engine produce one description of the repo's remote state, then hand-copies most of it into a second, differently-shaped struct just so the presentation function can read it. Every field that exists in both places is a field two types have to agree about, and a translation step that can silently drop or mistranslate one. The second struct earns its keep for exactly three things the first doesn't carry: whether a workroom is even selected, whether it's a repo at all, and the repo's pull-rebase setting.

Stakes if we pick wrong: keeping both means every new piece of remote state gets added in two places plus the mapping between them, and the translation is untested surface sitting between two tested layers. Collapsing wrongly means the pure, easily-testable mapper starts depending on a bigger engine type and gets harder to construct in tests.

Recommendation: A — one struct, with the three presentation-only facts as parameters to the mapper rather than mirrored fields. The mapper stays pure and the duplication goes away. Directly maps to your "flag repetition aggressively" preference.

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. Four implementations after this plan; toolbar uses a `??` fallback between two of them.

questions.question:
D10 — How should the "reading a branch label spawns zero VCS calls" guarantee be tested? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-test-gaps>

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. D9 routes four surfaces through one branch source; `AppStore.swift:1232-1234` documents the current property: "Reuses the already-resolved sidebar caches … so it adds no new VCS calls."

ELI10: Right now the sidebar and status bar get the branch name for free — they read a value some other resolver already computed. Your D9 choice unifies all four surfaces onto one source, and the naive way to do that is to have each surface ask the resolver. That would turn a free read into a repository read per project, per render. This codebase has already been burned by exactly that shape: the recorded pitfall `history-eager-focus-is-a-full-vcs-read` (9/10, cross-model) documents how an innocent-looking focus call turned out to be a full revwalk and starved the thread pool. The fix is that the resolver WRITES a shared cache and all four surfaces READ it — but nothing currently stops a future edit from reintroducing the direct call.

Stakes if we pick wrong: without a guard, the regression is invisible in tests and shows up as the History-loads-forever symptom under a burst of selections — the hardest class of bug in this app to diagnose, and one you've already paid for once.

Recommendation: A — a counting stub that fails if a label read touches the provider. It's the only test that actually pins the property, and it's cheap because the injection seam already exists on every resolver in this codebase.

options.label: Counting stub provider, assert zero calls (recommended)
options.description:
Extend `BranchLabelTests` with a stub `VCSProviding` that increments a counter per call. Read `branchLabel` for a root and a workroom, assert the counter is 0. Keeps the 4 existing tests as the behaviour guard.

Completeness: 10/10

✅ Pins the actual invariant — not "the label is right" but "getting it cost nothing" — which is the property D9 puts at risk and no existing test covers.
✅ Cheap: the closure-injection seam is already the house pattern on `BranchResolver`, `DiffResolver` and `HistoryModel`, so the stub is a few lines.
✅ Fails loudly at the unit gate rather than surfacing as thread-pool starvation under load. (human: ~2h / CC: ~10min)

options.label: Assert it at the store level instead
options.description:
Test that `AppStore`'s unified accessor reads only from its dictionaries by asserting the cache is populated before any read returns non-nil.

Completeness: 7/10

✅ Tests the store's contract without needing a provider stub at all, so it stays close to the code that actually changed.
✅ Naturally covers the "nil until resolved" behaviour that `testNilWhenNoStatusResolved` already asserts.
❌ Proves the cache is used, not that the provider ISN'T — a surface that reads the cache AND opportunistically kicks a resolve would still pass.

options.label: No guard — rely on code review
options.description:
Implement the shared-cache shape, document the constraint in a comment, add no test.

Completeness: 4/10

✅ Zero test cost, and the constraint is at least written down where the next editor will read it.
✅ The 4 existing `BranchLabelTests` still guard the label values themselves.
❌ This is precisely how the recorded pitfall happened the first time — a documented-but-unenforced performance property, broken by an edit that looked harmless and only failed under a burst of selections.

content.text:
**`[P2] (confidence: 9/10)` — push, pull and switch have engine integration tests but no test at the UI tier.**

The plan's `file://`-remote integration tests prove the engine performs each op correctly. The XCUITest list covers read states plus fetch. Nothing exercises *click sync when ahead → push happens → counts clear*, the dirty-tree confirmation before pull, or the error escalation path. 5 of the 19 gaps are these flows.

questions.question:
D11 — Cover the push / pull / switch user flows at the UI tier? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-test-flows>

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. Plan has 9 XCUITests covering read states + fetch; push/pull/switch are engine-tested only.

ELI10: There are two different questions a test can answer. "Does `git push` run correctly with the right arguments in the right directory?" — the integration tests answer that against a throwaway local remote. And "when the user clicks the segment that says Push origin, does a push actually happen, does the button disable while it runs, and do the counts clear afterwards?" — nothing answers that. The wiring between the button and the engine is exactly where a plan this size tends to break: a missing await, an action mapped to the wrong enum case, a confirmation dialog that swallows the click.

Stakes if we pick wrong: the engine is proven and the UI is proven, but the seam between them ships unverified — so a mis-wired action means clicking "Push origin" silently does nothing, or worse, fires the pull path. That's a bug you'd only find by using it, on the one code path that mutates a repo.

Recommendation: A — extend the fixture to record which action was requested and let tests assert the wiring. This is the boil-the-ocean call: with the fixture seam already built for the read states, adding action recording is small, and it covers the five highest-consequence flows in the feature.

options.label: Fixture records actions; add 5 flow tests (recommended)
options.description:
Extend the fixture provider to record requested actions and return seeded outcomes. Add UITests for: ahead→push→counts clear, behind+dirty→confirm→pull, switch→branch changes, auth failure→inline error, and second-click-while-in-flight is dropped.

Completeness: 10/10

✅ Covers the button-to-engine seam, which neither the integration tests nor the current UITests touch, on the only code paths in this feature that mutate a repository.
✅ The fixture seam and launch-argument plumbing already exist for the read states, so this is seeded outcomes plus an action log — not new infrastructure.
✅ Catches the specific failure the plan is most exposed to: 13 presentation states mapping to 5 actions, where one wrong mapping is invisible until a user clicks it. (human: ~1 day / CC: ~25min)

options.label: Add 2 flow tests — push and the in-flight guard
options.description:
Fixture action recording, but only test ahead→push→counts clear and the double-click drop.

Completeness: 7/10

✅ Covers the single most-used mutating flow and the re-entrancy guard, which are the two most likely to be exercised on day one.
✅ Roughly half the fixture work, and the recording seam it builds makes the other three trivial to add later.

# Test Plan
Generated by /plan-eng-review on 2026-07-31
Branch: master
Repo: joelmoss/workroom
Feature: VCS toolbar (branch dropdown + push/pull/fetch status + fetch button)

## Affected Surfaces
- Right inspector, Changes section active — the new 3-segment toolbar above the "Changes" header. Verify it appears ONLY when Changes is the active activity section, never on Files.
- Right inspector at 260pt (minimum) and 520pt (maximum) width — the degradation ladder.
- Branch dropdown popover (300x360) — filter field, LOCAL/REMOTE groups, current-branch checkmark.
- Terminal status bar + project sidebar + Changes panel branch capsule — all now read one unified branch source; verify none regressed.
- Menu bar: new "Source Control" menu (Fetch, Push, Pull, Switch Branch...).

## Key Interactions to Verify
- Click the branch segment -> popover opens, filter is focused, typing narrows the list, arrow keys move, Return switches.
- Click the middle segment when ahead -> pushes; button disables and shows a spinner; ahead count clears on success.
- Click the middle segment when behind -> pulls with rebase; if the working tree is dirty a confirmation appears first.
- Click the fetch icon -> spinner, then "Last fetched just now"; the timestamp then ticks (30s cadence).
- Second click while an action is in flight -> dropped, not queued.
- Fetch in one workroom -> the "last fetched" label updates for every workroom of that project (it is per-project by design).
- Run `git fetch` / `jj git fetch` in the workroom's own terminal -> the toolbar's label updates without any in-app action.
- Switch the active section to Files and back -> toolbar hides and reappears; no work is done while hidden.

## Edge Cases
- Repo with no remote -> "No remote configured", all actions disabled.
- Branch never pushed -> "Publish branch", not "Push origin". THIS IS THE WORKROOM DEFAULT (worktrees have no upstream).
- Diverged (ahead AND behind) -> primary action is Pull, badges show behind-then-ahead.
- Never fetched -> "Never fetched", no timestamp. Distinct from unreadable, which shows no timestamp at all.
- Filter text matching zero branches -> empty-state, not a blank list.
- Branch already checked out in a sibling workroom -> row disabled for git (switch would fail); advisory only for jj.
- jj workroom with an unbookmarked working copy -> Push uses jj's anonymous-branch path and creates a `push-<id>` bookmark.
- jj working copy that is empty and undescribed -> push targets the parent commit, not the empty working copy.
- Detached HEAD (git) -> no counts, no Publish.
- Inspector at 260pt -> the "Current Branch" caption drops; nothing clips; height stays fixed.
- HTTPS remote with no credential helper -> immediate auth error with actionable copy, NOT a long spinner.
- SSH remote with a passphrase-protected key and no ssh-agent -> immediate failure, NOT a 120-300s hang.
- Two windows on two workrooms of the same project, acting at once -> operations serialize; no wedged rebase.
- Pull that produces conflicts (jj) -> reported as conflicted even though the command exits zero.
- Interrupted pull -> if a rebase is left in progress, the error says to run `git rebase --abort` and does NOT offer Retry.

## Critical Paths
- Open inspector -> read correct branch, ahead/behind counts, and last-fetch time for both a git and a jj workroom.
- Ahead -> Push -> counts clear (the most-used mutating flow).
- Behind + dirty tree -> confirm -> Pull with rebase -> local commits land on top, uncommitted work preserved.
- Open dropdown -> filter -> switch branch -> every branch-displaying surface agrees on the new name.
- Any network failure -> the user sees a specific, actionable message and can retry or knows what to fix.
EOF
echo "WROTE: $OUT"; wc -l "$OUT"

content.text:
## Section 4 — Performance review

**`[P2] (confidence: 9/10)` — the ref list is per-*project* data fetched per-*workroom*, and my plan contradicts itself about when it loads.**

Two statements in the plan disagree. The engine section folds the ref list into `resolveState` (it comes from the same `for-each-ref` / `bookmark list` that yields ahead/behind). The UI section says *"Branch list is loaded only when the popover opens … never on selection change."* Both can't hold. And either way the data is repo-shared: N workrooms of one project each re-enumerate the same refs on their own 15s TTL.

questions.question:
D12 — How should the ref list be scoped and cached? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-perf>

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. Measured: jj `bookmark list` ~72ms on a 30-bookmark repo (mostly process startup); git `for-each-ref` ~30ms.

ELI10: Branches belong to the repository, not to a workroom — all of a project's workrooms are worktrees sharing one set of refs. The plan currently attaches the ref list to the per-workroom state, so clicking through ten workrooms of one project runs the same enumeration ten times and caches ten copies of the same answer. Separately, the plan says two contradictory things about when the list loads: the engine section gets it for free alongside the ahead/behind counts (one command returns both), while the UI section claims it only loads when the dropdown opens. The engine section is right — you cannot get the current branch's counts without the command that also returns every other ref — so the lazy-load sentence is simply wrong and should go.

Stakes if we pick wrong: leaving it per-workroom is a real but modest waste — tens of milliseconds per selection and a few duplicate copies in memory. Leaving the contradiction in the plan is worse: whoever implements it picks one reading, and if they pick the lazy one they will add a second command to get the counts, doubling the process spawns for no gain.

Recommendation: A — one command as the engine section describes, cached per project root rather than per workroom, and delete the lazy-load sentence. Maps to your DRY preference: one read, one cache, N readers.

options.label: Cache per project root; delete the lazy-load claim (recommended)
options.description:
Keep the single command. Store the ref list keyed by project root with its own 15s TTL, shared by every workroom of that project. Per-workroom state keeps only the current ref and its tracking. Remove the contradictory "popover-only" sentence.

Completeness: 10/10

✅ One enumeration serves every workroom of a project, so clicking through the sidebar stops re-reading identical data and memory holds one copy instead of N.
✅ Resolves the contradiction in the direction that is actually achievable — the counts and the list come from the same process, so there is nothing to defer.
✅ Matches how the app already models repo-shared facts: `rootRefs` is keyed by project, not by workroom. (human: ~3h / CC: ~15min)

options.label: Keep per-workroom; just fix the contradiction
options.description:
Leave the ref list on the per-workroom state as planned, and delete the incorrect lazy-load sentence so the single-command design is unambiguous.

Completeness: 7/10

✅ Smallest change to an already-large plan — removes one wrong sentence and nothing else.
✅ Per-workroom keying is simpler to reason about: one state object, one lifetime, no second cache to invalidate.
❌ Keeps re-reading repo-shared data once per workroom selection, and the plan itself already flagged this as phase-4 work — so it ships a known inefficiency with a TODO attached.

options.label: Two commands: narrow read + lazy full list
options.description:
A cheap command for just the current branch's tracking on every refresh, plus the full ref enumeration only when the popover opens.

Completeness: 6/10

✅ Genuinely minimises what the frequent path reads — one ref instead of up to 500, which matters on a repo with thousands of branches.
✅ Makes the popover's cost explicit and user-triggered.
❌ Two process spawns instead of one on any refresh where the popover is open, and process startup dominates the measured cost — so it is probably slower in practice, for more code.

Verified the load-bearing claims empirically (git 2.55, jj 0.43, real repos) plus the cited source lines. Findings below; **[V]** = verified in repo/shell, **[R]** = reasoning-only.

---

### P1

**1. [V] The `%(push:short)`/`%(push:track)` premise — "the whole ballgame" (plan:88-92) — is false on a default git config.**
`branch_get_push` under `push.default=simple` resolves the upstream *first* and bails if there is none. Measured:
```
push.default=simple    REF=feat2 UP=[] PUSH=[]                PUSHT=[]
push.default=current   REF=feat2 UP=[] PUSH=[origin/feat2]    PUSHT=[[gone]]
push.default=upstream  REF=feat2 UP=[] PUSH=[]                PUSHT=[]
push.default=nothing   REF=feat2 UP=[] PUSH=[]                PUSHT=[]
```
Only `current`/`matching` work. `git config --get push.default` on this machine returns **`current`** — that is why it appeared to work. `simple` is git's built-in default. Consequence: on a stock machine every `git worktree add -b` workroom (`internal/vcs/git.go:30`) gets *no* push ref, and the stated fallback (`upstream:*`) is also empty → the feature's headline number is permanently blank for the plan's own primary case. Fix: stop deriving this from `%(push)`; look up `refs/remotes/<remote>/<branch>` in the same `for-each-ref` output and compute divergence, or spend one `rev-list --left-right --count`.

**2. [V] The plan's own integration test disproves the mechanism.** plan:592 sets `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null`; plan:599-600 asserts `%(push:short) == origin/<branch>` for a worktree. With that env, `push.default` falls to built-in `simple` → measured `PUSH=[]` for both a no-upstream and a local-upstream branch. The test written to pin the semantics will fail.

**3. [V] Even where `%(push)` resolves, `%(push:track)` is `[gone]`, not a count** (measured above). So state row 4 ("Publish branch", badge `N ↑`, plan:324) has no `N` — and the plan's own `gone ⇒ counts nil` rule (plan:218) makes it unfillable from this one command.

**4. [V] Fetch-at-root + read-FETCH_HEAD-per-worktree ⇒ every workroom reads "never fetched", forever.** plan:103 fetches at the project root; plan:190 resolves the gitdir by following `.git`-as-file into `.git/worktrees/<n>/`. I backdated `.git/worktrees/wt1/FETCH_HEAD` to 2020, ran `git fetch` at the root:
```
after root fetch:  root=Jul 31 20:52:58 2026    wt1 =Jan  1 00:00:00 2020
```
Fetching *inside* wt1 wrote only `.git/worktrees/wt1/FETCH_HEAD` and never created `.git/FETCH_HEAD`. plan:193-196 asserts the opposite, three lines after stating the rule that breaks it. Read the **root's** FETCH_HEAD for workrooms.

**5. [V] jj: clicking the branch that's already shown as current strands the workroom's work and deletes files from disk, with zero visible change in the toolbar.** Reproduced on jj 0.43: `jj workspace add --name wr1` → `@` unbookmarked, nearest ancestor bookmark `main`, so the toolbar reads "main" and the picker checkmarks `main`. Then `jj new main`:
```
before:  ykmwswrsykrm {}      [wip in wr1]      <- b.txt on disk
         ltymklkxytnm {main}  [base]
jj new main -> "Added 0 files, modified 0 files, removed 1 files"
after:   vsvxzuwqvwzy {}      []                <- new @
         ykmwswrsykrm {}      [wip in wr1]      <- nameless dangling head
```
`b.txt` is gone from the working copy, the old work is reachable only by change id, and segment 1 still says "main". The plan specifies no `target == current` guard, and for jj that is precisely the destructive case.

**6. [V] For jj, "current branch" is not a property of the workroom at all**, so segment 1 displays and offers to mutate a shared value. In the repro, the project root's `@` (`lmuwuykmtzqo`) *and* wr1's `@` both report `main`. Five workrooms → five toolbars all reading "main". The unified git/jj toolbar is forcing a git model: for jj, segment 1's value is an ancestor bookmark common to N workrooms and "switching" it creates a commit. Either show the change/description for jj, or make segment 1 a *bookmark-creation* affordance.

**7. [V] Strategically: branch switching is product-negative and duplicates an affordance the app already ships correctly.**
- Workroom identity is the directory basename (`internal/vcs/git.go:70-80` → `filepath.Base(path)`); no `branch` key anywhere in `internal/config/`. After a switch, the sidebar name and the new toolbar disagree permanently and nothing reconciles them.
- The picker must disable every branch checked out in a sibling workroom (plan:461). The more the user uses the product as designed, the more of the dropdown is greyed out.
- `macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/OpenWorkroomDialog.swift` is already the filterable, project-grouped picker for "go work on that other thing" (⌘O). The plan clones its UI verbatim (plan:449-452) while swapping its *product-correct* action for `git switch`.
Recommendation: cut the switch. Make segment 1 a read-only label whose click opens the existing Open-Workroom picker, or "New workroom from branch…".

**8. [R] The most-likely pull outcome has no in-app recovery.** plan:115 states workroom trees are *always* dirty ⇒ `--autostash` always engages ⇒ a rebase conflict leaves `.git/rebase-merge`, the autostash unapplied, and the plan's answer is `.rebaseInProgress` with "must **not** offer Retry" (plan:257) and no abort/continue affordance. The expected case dumps the user into a half-rebased worktree with a 10pt inline error. If pull ships, `git rebase --abort` must be a button.

---

### P2

**9. [V] The degradation ladder inverts the staleness honesty.** The count pill "never yields (`.fixedSize()`)" (plan:435) while "Last fetched N ago" is the *first* thing abbreviated (plan:430) and the caption drops at 260pt (plan:432). At the plan's own design floor the unverified number survives and the caveat degrades. Combine with "auto-fetch: **Never**" (plan:36) + one-click push and the three decisions jointly maximise the `.rejected` rate. GitHub Desktop — the stated model — auto-fetches. Either auto-fetch on inspector focus (you already gate everything on visibility) or fetch-then-act inside the push/pull handlers. "Last fetched N ago" is not sufficient honesty when it's the first thing the layout drops.

**10. [V] One shared `--count` cap across `refs/heads` + `refs/remotes`, sorted by committerdate, silently drops local branches.** Measured on a repo with 12 remote refs: `--sort=-committerdate --count=5 refs/heads refs/remotes` returned **1 local + 4 remote**. With `refCap: 500` (plan:61) a repo with 500+ remote refs can show an empty LOCAL group, and the filter field searches a client-side truncated list — so "hundreds of branches", the stated reason for `.popover` over `Menu` (plan:443), is exactly the case the cap breaks. Separate caps per namespace.

**11. [V] A branch whose upstream is a LOCAL branch produces nonsense.** Measured: `UP=[main] UPT=[[ahead 3]] PUSH=[]`. The `push:* → upstream:*` fallback (plan:91) then sets `comparedTo = "main"` and renders "Push origin · 3 ↑" for divergence from a *local* ref; the pull command built from `comparedTo` (plan:114) becomes `git pull --rebase <remote=main> <branch=nothing>`. Nothing checks that `%(upstream)` is under `refs/remotes/`.

**12. [V] Every UI string hardcodes "origin"; the push remote need not be origin.** Measured: `-c remote.pushDefault=upstream` → `PUSH=[upstream/feature-nou]`. plan rows 4/6/7/8/9/10-12 all say "origin" ("Push origin", "Pull origin with rebase", "isn't on origin yet", "from/to origin"), and `primaryRemote`'s derivation is never specified. Fork workflows read a label naming the wrong remote.

**13. [V] Routing git writes through `JJSnapshotGate` doesn't close the contention it targets, because git *reads* aren't gated.** `WorkroomStatusResolver.resolveGit` (`:98`) never touches `self.gate`; only `resolveJJ` does (`:142`). The gate's own doc cites `packed-refs.lock could not be obtained` from concurrent git-worktree access. A fetch/push writing `packed-refs` while the ungated status sweep runs `git status` across N sibling workrooms reproduces it exactly. Either gate git reads too, or accept `.locked` and retry.

**14. [V] Auth does not "come free", and the risk is env, not entitlements.** On the entitlements question you asked: `project.yml:267` `ENABLE_HARDENED_RUNTIME: YES`, `:296-299` "The app needs no entitlements" + `CODE_SIGN_INJECT_BASE_ENTITLEMENTS: NO`, no `.entitlements` file, no App Sandbox — spawning `/usr/bin/env git`/`ssh` from the signed notarized app is fine. **The real gap:** `StatusCommandRunner.swift:50-51` builds the child env from `ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment` (the launchd GUI env) and overrides **only** `PATH`. The shell-probed full env exists (`ShellEnvironment.environment()`, `:292`) and is deliberately reserved for setup/teardown scripts (`WorkroomCLI.swift:320`). So anything set in `.zshrc` is invisible: `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` (1Password / gpg-agent SSH agents — very common), `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`. Those users hit `.authRequired` and get told to configure a credential helper they already have. Also missing from the classify table (plan:242): `Host key verification failed` — with `BatchMode` and no tty, a first connect to a new host hard-fails into `.other` with raw stderr. And the "matches the `gh` precedent" argument is weak: `gh` carries its own OAuth token in its own config and proves nothing about credential helpers or ssh-agent.

**15. [V] A dirty `git switch` silently drags uncommitted work onto the other branch, and the mitigation guarantees confirmation fatigue.** Measured: staged `carried.txt`, `git switch feature-nou`, `git status --short` → `A carried.txt` on the new branch. plan:499 confirms "only when the working tree is dirty" — but plan:115 says workroom trees are *always* dirty, so the dialog fires on every switch, and its copy isn't specified to say the changes will travel.

**16. [R] Hooks and hard-kill aftermath are unmodelled.** `git switch` runs `post-checkout`; `git pull --rebase` runs `post-rewrite`/`post-merge` — arbitrary user scripts, now running from a GUI app with the launchd env and SIGTERM at timeout / `ProcessTree.killTree` at +2s (`StatusCommandRunner.swift:88-98`). A `post-checkout` that runs a package manager gets SIGKILLed at 120s. The plan probes for `rebase-merge` after a timed-out pull but never for the `index.lock` a SIGKILLed git leaves — which then breaks every subsequent *read* for that workroom. `git switch` has no `--no-verify`; suppress via `-c core.hooksPath=` in the existing `gitHardening` mechanism if that's the intent, and probe for stale `index.lock`.

**17. [V] No `git`/`jj` version floor, and `for-each-ref` fails atomically on an unknown atom.** Measured: `git for-each-ref --format='%(bogusatom)'` → `fatal: unknown field name: bogusatom`, no partial output. The app bundles neither binary (`ShellEnvironment.path()` takes whatever's on PATH). Everything is verified against git 2.55 / jj 0.43 only; `jj bookmark` was `jj branch` pre-0.18 and `tracking_*_count()` is newer. One old tool ⇒ the whole feature is `.other` with raw stderr. Needs a version probe and a legible "needs git ≥ X" state.

**18. [R] jj `rebase` rewrites the shared repo; sibling workspaces go stale and nothing surfaces it.** All workrooms of a jj project share one repo/op-store (per `JJSnapshotGate`'s own doc). `jj rebase -b @` rewrites commits; any other workspace whose `@` descends from a rewritten commit is marked stale and needs `jj workspace update-stale` before its next command — which will surface in the app as a mystery error in a *different* workroom than the one the user acted in. The plan's only cross-workroom consideration is gate serialization. Also `-b @` moves the whole branch containing `@`, which can reach commits the user considers another workroom's when they share a non-trunk base.

**19. [R] jj `--change` bookmarks accumulate into the picker's LOCAL group.** Every push of an unbookmarked `@` mints a permanent `push-<changeid>` (plan:158). After a week the LOCAL group is a wall of `push-qzvltpmk` rows. Also an unresolved asymmetry: git is "**Never** `--force`" (plan:112) while re-pushing an amended change via `--change` moves the bookmark non-fast-forward by design.

**20. [V] The plan text contradicts three of the nine review decisions**, so a literal implementation reintroduces what was cut: plan:313 still takes `VCSSyncSnapshot` (decision 7 collapsed it); plan:218 + plan:222 still declare `pullFrom` and `hasUnbookmarkedWork` and plan:91/114 still *use* `pullFrom` (decision 2 cut both); plan:226 + plan:246 still carry `.noUpstream` and state row 4 keys off it (decision 2 cut it). Update the file or the decisions are lost on implementation.

**21. [R] Strategic: there's a much cheaper 80%.** Read-only status + one Fetch button is one `for-each-ref` (fixed per finding 1), one mtime, one `git fetch`, one label, one pill. It needs no `VCSWriting`, no write gating, no `--autostash`, no rebase recovery, no confirmation dialogs, no picker, no `CommandMenu`/`isAppShortcut`/focused-value plumbing, and none of jj's `--change`/`jj new` semantics — i.e. it drops findings 5, 7, 8, 15, 16, 18, 19 entirely. Push/pull/switch carry all the risk and most of the spec, and the user has a real terminal in the same window one keystroke away where they already work with real output and real prompts. Ship read-only + fetch; let usage decide whether push belongs in-app.

---

### P3

**22. [V] Segment 3 duplicates segment 2 in the common case.** States 5 and 6 make the *sync* segment's click a fetch (plan:326-327), and segment 3 is also a fetch. Two adjacent controls, identical behaviour, in the state the user is in most of the time. GitHub Desktop's fetch lives *inside* the sync button, not beside it.

**23. [V] The layout machinery is disproportionate to fitting two strings in a 260pt column.** `ViewThatFits` has **zero** existing uses (`grep -rn ViewThatFits WorkroomApp/` → nothing), plus a `titleVariants: [String]` ladder with a test asserting strictly-decreasing lengths, 4 abbreviation levels for one title, 12 named metrics, and an arithmetic assertion `branchMin + syncMin + fetchWidth + 2 <= 260`. The stated blocker for the simpler placement (`SectionHeader`'s trailing accessory, where Refresh already lives) is that it sits behind an `NSHostingController` that doesn't inherit `@EnvironmentObject` (plan:488) — but `ChangesPanel.swift:19-21` documents that headers and bodies are already **environment-injected** across that boundary. Soft blocker.

**24. [R] The 13-state hand-ordered precedence (`13 > 10-12 > 1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 9 > 8 > 7 > 5 > 6`) is a bug farm.** It's really 3 orthogonal axes — target validity, in-flight, divergence. Model the axes; the total order will fall out.

**25. [V] Build order ships dead UI.** Steps 6-7 land the toolbar and the branch picker; step 8 lands the actions. So the picker ships as a dropdown that can't switch and the sync segment as a button that can't push. Interleave: each action lands with its own affordance.

Either show the change/description for jj, or make segment 1 a *bookmark-creation* affordance.

**7. [V] Strategically: branch switching is product-negative and duplicates an affordance the app already ships correctly.**
- Workroom identity is the directory basename (`internal/vcs/git.go:70-80` → `filepath.Base(path)`); no `branch` key anywhere in `internal/config/`. After a switch, the sidebar name and the new toolbar disagree permanently and nothing reconciles them.
- The picker must disable every branch checked out in a sibling workroom (plan:461). The more the user uses the product as designed, the more of the dropdown is greyed out.
- `macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/OpenWorkroomDialog.swift` is already the filterable, project-grouped picker for "go work on that other thing" (⌘O). The plan clones its UI verbatim (plan:449-452) while swapping its *product-correct* action for `git switch`.
Recommendation: cut the switch. Make segment 1 a read-only label whose click opens the existing Open-Workroom picker, or "New workroom from branch…".

**8. [R] The most-likely pull outcome has no in-app recovery.** plan:115 states workroom trees are *always* dirty ⇒ `--autostash` always engages ⇒ a rebase conflict leaves `.git/rebase-merge`, the autostash unapplied, and the plan's answer is `.rebaseInProgress` with "must **not** offer Retry" (plan:257) and no abort/continue affordance. The expected case dumps the user into a half-rebased worktree with a 10pt inline error. If pull ships, `git rebase --abort` must be a button.

---

### P2

**9. [V] The degradation ladder inverts the staleness honesty.** The count pill "never yields (`.fixedSize()`)" (plan:435) while "Last fetched N ago" is the *first* thing abbreviated (plan:430) and the caption drops at 260pt (plan:432). At the plan's own design floor the unverified number survives and the caveat degrades. Combine with "auto-fetch: **Never**" (plan:36) + one-click push and the three decisions jointly maximise the `.rejected` rate. GitHub Desktop — the stated model — auto-fetches. Either auto-fetch on inspector focus (you already gate everything on visibility) or fetch-then-act inside the push/pull handlers. "Last fetched N ago" is not sufficient honesty when it's the first thing the layout drops.

**10. [V] One shared `--count` cap across `refs/heads` + `refs/remotes`, sorted by committerdate, silently drops local branches.** Measured on a repo with 12 remote refs: `--sort=-committerdate --count=5 refs/heads refs/remotes` returned **1 local + 4 remote**. With `refCap: 500` (plan:61) a repo with 500+ remote refs can show an empty LOCAL group, and the filter field searches a client-side truncated list — so "hundreds of branches", the stated reason for `.popover` over `Menu` (plan:443), is exactly the case the cap breaks. Separate caps per namespace.

**11. [V] A branch whose upstream is a LOCAL branch produces nonsense.** Measured: `UP=[main] UPT=[[ahead 3]] PUSH=[]`. The `push:* → upstream:*` fallback (plan:91) then sets `comparedTo = "main"` and renders "Push origin · 3 ↑" for divergence from a *local* ref; the pull command built from `comparedTo` (plan:114) becomes `git pull --rebase <remote=main> <branch=nothing>`. Nothing checks that `%(upstream)` is under `refs/remotes/`.

**12. [V] Every UI string hardcodes "origin"; the push remote need not be origin.** Measured: `-c remote.pushDefault=upstream` → `PUSH=[upstream/feature-nou]`. plan rows 4/6/7/8/9/10-12 all say "origin" ("Push origin", "Pull origin with rebase", "isn't on origin yet", "from/to origin"), and `primaryRemote`'s derivation is never specified. Fork workflows read a label naming the wrong remote.

**13. [V] Routing git writes through `JJSnapshotGate` doesn't close the contention it targets, because git *reads* aren't gated.** `WorkroomStatusResolver.resolveGit` (`:98`) never touches `self.gate`; only `resolveJJ` does (`:142`). The gate's own doc cites `packed-refs.lock could not be obtained` from concurrent git-worktree access. A fetch/push writing `packed-refs` while the ungated status sweep runs `git status` across N sibling workrooms reproduces it exactly. Either gate git reads too, or accept `.locked` and retry.

**14. [V] Auth does not "come free", and the risk is env, not entitlements.** On the entitlements question you asked: `project.yml:267` `ENABLE_HARDENED_RUNTIME: YES`, `:296-299` "The app needs no entitlements" + `CODE_SIGN_INJECT_BASE_ENTITLEMENTS: NO`, no `.entitlements` file, no App Sandbox — spawning `/usr/bin/env git`/`ssh` from the signed notarized app is fine. **The real gap:** `StatusCommandRunner.swift:50-51` builds the child env from `ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment` (the launchd GUI env) and overrides **only** `PATH`. The shell-probed full env exists (`ShellEnvironment.environment()`, `:292`) and is deliberately reserved for setup/teardown scripts (`WorkroomCLI.swift:320`). So anything set in `.zshrc` is invisible: `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` (1Password / gpg-agent SSH agents — very common), `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`. Those users hit `.authRequired` and get told to configure a credential helper they already have. Also missing from the classify table (plan:242): `Host key verification failed` — with `BatchMode` and no tty, a first connect to a new host hard-fails into `.other` with raw stderr. And the "matches the `gh` precedent" argument is weak: `gh` carries its own OAuth token in its own config and proves nothing about credential helpers or ssh-agent.

**15. [V] A dirty `git switch` silently drags uncommitted work onto the other branch, and the mitigation guarantees confirmation fatigue.** Measured: staged `carried.txt`, `git switch feature-nou`, `git status --short` → `A carried.txt` on the new branch. plan:499 confirms "only when the working tree is dirty" — but plan:115 says workroom trees are *always* dirty, so the dialog fires on every switch, and its copy isn't specified to say the changes will travel.

**16. [R] Hooks and hard-kill aftermath are unmodelled.** `git switch` runs `post-checkout`; `git pull --rebase` runs `post-rewrite`/`post-merge` — arbitrary user scripts, now running from a GUI app with the launchd env and SIGTERM at timeout / `ProcessTree.killTree` at +2s (`StatusCommandRunner.swift:88-98`). A `post-checkout` that runs a package manager gets SIGKILLed at 120s. The plan probes for `rebase-merge` after a timed-out pull but never for the `index.lock` a SIGKILLed git leaves — which then breaks every subsequent *read* for that workroom. `git switch` has no `--no-verify`; suppress via `-c core.hooksPath=` in the existing `gitHardening` mechanism if that's the intent, and probe for stale `index.lock`.

**17. [V] No `git`/`jj` version floor, and `for-each-ref` fails atomically on an unknown atom.** Measured: `git for-each-ref --format='%(bogusatom)'` → `fatal: unknown field name: bogusatom`, no partial output. The app bundles neither binary (`ShellEnvironment.path()` takes whatever's on PATH). Everything is verified against git 2.55 / jj 0.43 only; `jj bookmark` was `jj branch` pre-0.18 and `tracking_*_count()` is newer. One old tool ⇒ the whole feature is `.other` with raw stderr. Needs a version probe and a legible "needs git ≥ X" state.

**18. [R] jj `rebase` rewrites the shared repo; sibling workspaces go stale and nothing surfaces it.** All workrooms of a jj project share one repo/op-store (per `JJSnapshotGate`'s own doc). `jj rebase -b @` rewrites commits; any other workspace whose `@` descends from a rewritten commit is marked stale and needs `jj workspace update-stale` before its next command — which will surface in the app as a mystery error in a *different* workroom than the one the user acted in. The plan's only cross-workroom consideration is gate serialization. Also `-b @` moves the whole branch containing `@`, which can reach commits the user considers another workroom's when they share a non-trunk base.

**19. [R] jj `--change` bookmarks accumulate into the picker's LOCAL group.** Every push of an unbookmarked `@` mints a permanent `push-<changeid>` (plan:158). After a week the LOCAL group is a wall of `push-qzvltpmk` rows. Also an unresolved asymmetry: git is "**Never** `--force`" (plan:112) while re-pushing an amended change via `--change` moves the bookmark non-fast-forward by design.

**20. [V] The plan text contradicts three of the nine review decisions**, so a literal implementation reintroduces what was cut: plan:313 still takes `VCSSyncSnapshot` (decision 7 collapsed it); plan:218 + plan:222 still declare `pullFrom` and `hasUnbookmarkedWork` and plan:91/114 still *use* `pullFrom` (decision 2 cut both); plan:226 + plan:246 still carry `.noUpstream` and state row 4 keys off it (decision 2 cut it). Update the file or the decisions are lost on implementation.

**21. [R] Strategic: there's a much cheaper 80%.** Read-only status + one Fetch button is one `for-each-ref` (fixed per finding 1), one mtime, one `git fetch`, one label, one pill. It needs no `VCSWriting`, no write gating, no `--autostash`, no rebase recovery, no confirmation dialogs, no picker, no `CommandMenu`/`isAppShortcut`/focused-value plumbing, and none of jj's `--change`/`jj new` semantics — i.e. it drops findings 5, 7, 8, 15, 16, 18, 19 entirely. Push/pull/switch carry all the risk and most of the spec, and the user has a real terminal in the same window one keystroke away where they already work with real output and real prompts. Ship read-only + fetch; let usage decide whether push belongs in-app.

---

### P3

**22. [V] Segment 3 duplicates segment 2 in the common case.** States 5 and 6 make the *sync* segment's click a fetch (plan:326-327), and segment 3 is also a fetch. Two adjacent controls, identical behaviour, in the state the user is in most of the time. GitHub Desktop's fetch lives *inside* the sync button, not beside it.

**23. [V] The layout machinery is disproportionate to fitting two strings in a 260pt column.** `ViewThatFits` has **zero** existing uses (`grep -rn ViewThatFits WorkroomApp/` → nothing), plus a `titleVariants: [String]` ladder with a test asserting strictly-decreasing lengths, 4 abbreviation levels for one title, 12 named metrics, and an arithmetic assertion `branchMin + syncMin + fetchWidth + 2 <= 260`. The stated blocker for the simpler placement (`SectionHeader`'s trailing accessory, where Refresh already lives) is that it sits behind an `NSHostingController` that doesn't inherit `@EnvironmentObject` (plan:488) — but `ChangesPanel.swift:19-21` documents that headers and bodies are already **environment-injected** across that boundary. Soft blocker.

**24. [R] The 13-state hand-ordered precedence (`13 > 10-12 > 1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 9 > 8 > 7 > 5 > 6`) is a bug farm.** It's really 3 orthogonal axes — target validity, in-flight, divergence. Model the axes; the total order will fall out.

**25. [V] Build order ships dead UI.** Steps 6-7 land the toolbar and the branch picker; step 8 lands the actions. So the picker ships as a dropdown that can't switch and the sync segment as a button that can't push. Interleave: each action lands with its own affordance.

content.text:
**Finding 4 CONFIRMED.** `git rev-parse --git-path FETCH_HEAD` returns `.git/FETCH_HEAD` from the root but `.git/worktrees/wr1/FETCH_HEAD` from the workroom. Fetching at the root does **not** write the workroom's copy. My plan fetches at the root *and* reads the per-worktree path — so every workroom would read "never fetched" forever.

## OUTSIDE VOICE (Claude subagent)

Codex timed out; the Claude subagent ran instead. 25 findings. **[V]** = it verified in-repo/shell, **[R]** = reasoning-only.

**P1**
1. **[V]** `%(push:short)`/`%(push:track)` is empty under `push.default=simple` (git's default) when there's no upstream. Only `current`/`matching` work. **I re-verified — confirmed.**
2. **[V]** The plan's own integration test (`GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null`) would therefore fail. **Confirmed.**
3. **[V]** Where `%(push)` does resolve with no upstream, `%(push:track)` is `[gone]`, not a count — so state 4's `N ↑` badge is unfillable.
4. **[V]** Fetch-at-root + read-per-worktree-`FETCH_HEAD` ⇒ every workroom reads "never fetched" forever. **I re-verified — confirmed.**
5. **[V]** jj: clicking the branch already shown as current runs `jj new main`, which strands the workroom's commit as a nameless head and **removes files from the working copy** — with no visible change in the toolbar. No `target == current` guard specified.
6. **[V]** For jj, "current branch" isn't a property of the workroom — N workrooms all report the same ancestor bookmark, so segment 1 displays and offers to mutate a shared value.
7. **[V]** Strategic: branch switching is product-negative — workroom identity is the directory basename (`internal/vcs/git.go:70-80`), no `branch` key in config, so sidebar and toolbar disagree permanently after a switch; and `OpenWorkroomDialog.swift` already ships the correct affordance.
8. **[R]** The most-likely pull outcome (dirty tree → `--autostash` → conflict) leaves a half-rebased worktree, and the plan forbids Retry with no abort affordance.

**P2**
9. **[V]** Degradation ladder inverts the honesty: the unverified count pill never yields, while "Last fetched N ago" abbreviates first. Combined with never-auto-fetch + one-click push, it maximises `.rejected`.
10. **[V]** One shared `--count` across `refs/heads`+`refs/remotes` sorted by date silently drops local branches (measured: 1 local + 4 remote at `--count=5`).
11. **[V]** A branch whose upstream is a *local* branch produces `comparedTo="main"` and a malformed pull command.
12. **[V]** Every UI string hardcodes "origin"; `remote.pushDefault` can make that wrong.
13. **[V]** Gating git *writes* doesn't close the contention, because git *reads* aren't gated (`WorkroomStatusResolver.resolveGit:98` never touches the gate).
14. **[V]** Auth doesn't "come free": entitlements are fine (`project.yml:267,296-299`, hardened runtime, no sandbox) but `StatusCommandRunner.swift:50-51` overrides only `PATH`, so `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` (1Password/gpg-agent), `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` from `.zshrc` are invisible. Also `Host key verification failed` is missing from the classify table.
15. **[V]** A dirty `git switch` silently carries uncommitted work to the other branch; the confirmation fires on every switch (trees are always dirty) and its copy doesn't say the changes travel.
16. **[R]** Hooks unmodelled — `post-checkout`/`post-rewrite` run user scripts from the GUI env and get SIGKILLed at timeout; no probe for the `index.lock` a killed git leaves, which breaks subsequent reads.
17. **[V]** No `git`/`jj` version floor; `for-each-ref` fails atomically on an unknown atom, so one old tool makes the whole feature `.other` with raw stderr.
18. **[R]** jj `rebase` rewrites the shared repo — sibling workspaces go stale and surface a mystery error in a *different* workroom.
19. **[R]** jj `--change` mints a permanent `push-<id>` per push; the LOCAL group fills with them.
20. **[V]** The plan file still contradicts three of the nine decisions (it hasn't been rewritten yet — that's on me, and I'm doing it).
21. **[R]** Strategic: read-only status + Fetch is a much cheaper 80% and drops findings 5, 7, 8, 15, 16, 18, 19 entirely.

**P3**
22. **[V]** Segment 3 duplicates segment 2 in states 5–6, where the sync segment's click is also a fetch.
23. **[V]** `ViewThatFits` has zero existing uses; the layout machinery is disproportionate, and the stated blocker for the simpler `SectionHeader` accessory placement is soft (headers *are* environment-injected — `ChangesPanel.swift:19-21`).
24. **[R]** The 13-state hand-ordered precedence is really 3 orthogonal axes; model the axes.
25. **[V]** Build order ships dead UI — the picker lands before switch works.

**CROSS-MODEL TENSION**
- **Scope**: My review took your settled full-scope decision as given and reviewed *how*. The outside voice argues switch and pull should be cut on product grounds (7, 21) and brings new switch/pull-specific risk (5, 8, 15, 16, 18, 19) that didn't exist when you decided. Presenting once, not re-litigating.
- **`%(push)` mechanism**: My Step 0 flagged the `push.default` wording as a doc nit. The outside voice showed it's a functional break. It's right; I under-read it.
- **D4 (gate git writes)**: I claimed it closes git contention. Finding 13 shows reads stay ungated, so it only half-closes it.

Six tensions need your call. First, the one that breaks the engine:

questions.question:
D13 — How should ahead/behind actually be computed, now that `%(push:track)` is confirmed broken? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-ov-pushtrack>

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. Verified by me just now on git 2.55: with `push.default=simple` (git's built-in default), a branch with no upstream gives `PUSH=[]` and `PUSHT=[]`. Only `current` and `matching` populate it. This machine is set to `current`, which is the sole reason the plan's measurement looked convincing.

ELI10: The plan's efficiency claim was that a single `git for-each-ref` returns the branch list AND how far ahead/behind each branch is, because git's `%(push:track)` field figures out the remote counterpart for you. It turns out that field gives up when a branch has no upstream configured, on git's default setting. Every Workroom workroom is created with `git worktree add -b`, which sets no upstream. So the feature's headline number — the "5 ↑" in your screenshot — would be blank for exactly the branches this product creates.

Stakes if we pick wrong: ship it as planned and the count pill is empty for every workroom on any machine that hasn't set `push.default=current`, while working perfectly on yours. That is the worst failure shape available: invisible in your own testing, broken for everyone else.

Recommendation: A — stop deriving counts from `%(push)`. Use the ref list for names and the current-branch marker, then one explicit `rev-list --left-right --count` against the remote counterpart. It's config-independent, exact, and per-row counts were already cut in D3 so we only need it for one branch.

options.label: One extra `rev-list --left-right --count` (recommended)
options.description:
`for-each-ref` still gives names, tips, `%(HEAD)`, `%(worktreepath)`. Counts come from one `git rev-list --left-right --count HEAD...refs/remotes/<remote>/<branch>`, with the remote counterpart resolved by name against the ref list we already have. Delete `%(push:*)` and `pullFrom` reasoning entirely.

Completeness: 10/10

✅ Config-independent — works identically under every `push.default`, so it cannot silently differ between your machine and a user's.
✅ Exact two-way counts from one cheap process, and it dissolves finding 11 (a local-branch upstream) because we only ever compare against `refs/remotes/`.
✅ Explicit over clever: the origin/same-name fallback becomes code you can read and test, not a git config side effect.
❌ Two processes per state read instead of one, so the plan's "one command answers everything" claim goes away. (human: ~3h / CC: ~15min)

options.label: Set `push.default` per-invocation to force it
options.description:
Pass `-c push.default=current` alongside the existing `gitHardening` flags so `%(push:*)` always resolves, keeping the single-command design.

Completeness: 6/10

✅ Keeps one process and the whole existing parse path — smallest change to the written plan.
✅ Deterministic regardless of user config, since we supply the value ourselves.
❌ `%(push:track)` still reports `[gone]` rather than a count when there's no remote branch yet, so state 4's badge stays unfillable — and we'd be reading a field whose meaning we've overridden, which is exactly the clever-over-explicit trap.

options.label: Require an upstream — set it on first push
options.description:
Show no counts until the branch has an upstream; `push --set-upstream` establishes one, after which `%(upstream:track)` works everywhere.

Completeness: 5/10

✅ Uses the field git actually intends for this, with no extra process and no config dependence.
✅ Honest: no upstream genuinely means there is nothing to compare against yet.
❌ A brand-new workroom — the product's core object, and the state users are in most often — shows no counts at all until they push once, so the toolbar is blank exactly when they most want to know they have unpushed work.

questions.question:
D14 — Scope re-check with new evidence: keep switch and pull, or cut them? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-ov-scope>

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. You chose full scope earlier; I am not re-litigating that on the same information. This is new information the outside voice produced and I verified.

ELI10: Three things came up that weren't on the table when you decided. First, in jj, clicking the branch the toolbar already shows as current runs `jj new main`, which was reproduced deleting a file from the working copy and leaving the workroom's commit as a nameless orphan — while the toolbar still reads "main". Second, a workroom's identity in your config is its directory name (`internal/vcs/git.go:70-80`); there is no branch field. So after a switch, the sidebar says one thing and the toolbar says another, permanently, and nothing reconciles them. Third, `OpenWorkroomDialog.swift` already is a filterable, project-grouped branch-ish picker bound to ⌘O — the plan clones its UI and swaps its product-correct action for `git switch`.

On pull: workroom trees are always dirty, so `--autostash` always engages, so the likely failure is a conflicted rebase that leaves a half-rebased worktree — and the plan forbids Retry with no abort button, sending the user to a terminal.

Stakes if we pick wrong: keeping switch means shipping a control that can silently destroy uncommitted jj work and permanently desynchronise a workroom's name from its branch. Cutting it means the dropdown becomes read-only or routes to the existing workroom picker, and you lose an affordance you asked for.

Recommendation: B — keep push and pull, cut switch. Push is unambiguously right for a workroom and the counts make it meaningful. Pull is recoverable if we add an abort button. Switch is the one whose product model actively fights the product: workrooms ARE branches, so switching one's branch makes its name a lie, and the jj path is destructive.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

options.label: Keep push + pull, cut switch (recommended)
options.description:
Segment 1 becomes a read-only branch label whose click opens the existing ⌘O workroom picker (or a "New workroom from branch…" action later). Push and pull stay; pull gains a `git rebase --abort` button.

✅ Drops findings 5, 7 and 15 outright — the jj data-loss path, the name/branch desync, and the always-firing dirty-switch confirmation — without losing anything you can't already do via ⌘O.
✅ Removes `BranchPickerPopover` and its switch plumbing: roughly 4 fewer gaps, one fewer new file, and the `checkedOutIn` disabled-row logic goes away with it.
✅ Keeps the two actions the counts actually motivate, so the toolbar still answers "am I ahead? push" and "am I behind? pull".

options.label: Keep everything, add the missing guards
options.description:
Full scope as decided. Add: a `target == current` no-op guard for jj switch, jj-specific copy explaining `jj new` semantics, dirty-switch copy that says changes travel with you, a `rebase --abort` button, and a stale-workspace notice for sibling jj workrooms.

✅ Delivers the toolbar you actually specified, including a dropdown that switches — which is what the GitHub Desktop model does and what you asked for.
✅ The identified risks all have concrete named mitigations rather than being unknowns; none of them is architecturally hard.
❌ The workroom-name-versus-branch desync has no fix short of renaming workrooms on switch, so the product model stays internally inconsistent, and jj segment 1 still shows a value shared by every workroom of the project. (human: ~2 days / CC: ~40min)

options.label: Cut switch and pull — read-only + fetch + push
options.description:
Toolbar shows branch, counts and last-fetch; Fetch and Push work; no pull, no switch.

✅ Drops findings 5, 7, 8, 15, 16, 18 and 19 — every destructive path — leaving only additive operations that cannot wedge a repo.
✅ Smallest surface that still delivers the screenshot's headline behaviour: "Push origin, 5 ↑, last fetched 9 minutes ago".
❌ "Pull origin with rebase" was explicitly in your ask, and being told you're 3 behind with no way to act on it is a worse state than not being told — it sends you to the terminal by design.

content.text:
**Switch is cut.** That dissolves findings 5, 6, 7, 10 and 15, deletes `BranchPickerPopover.swift`, the `checkedOutIn` field, `.alreadyCheckedOut`, the ⇧⌘B menu item, and two test gaps. Segment 1 becomes a read-only label routing to ⌘O. Pull gains an abort button.

Next — the confirmed `FETCH_HEAD` bug:

questions.question:
D15 — Which `FETCH_HEAD` should a workroom read? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-ov-fetchhead>

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. Verified by me: `git rev-parse --git-path FETCH_HEAD` returns `.git/FETCH_HEAD` at the project root but `.git/worktrees/wr1/FETCH_HEAD` inside a workroom. A root fetch does not write the workroom's copy.

ELI10: "Last fetched 9 minutes ago" is read from the timestamp of a file git writes when it fetches. The plan decided to always fetch at the project root, so that one fetch benefits every workroom — which is right. But it then reads that file from the workroom's own private git directory, and git gives each worktree its own copy. The root's fetch writes the root's file; the workroom's file is never created. So the label reads "Never fetched" forever, in every workroom, no matter how many times you fetch.

Stakes if we pick wrong: the single most visible string in the feature — the one in your screenshot — is permanently wrong for workrooms, which is where users spend all their time. It would look correct only when the inspector points at a project root.

Recommendation: A — resolve the shared git directory by stripping the `/worktrees/<name>` suffix we already have to parse anyway, and read its `FETCH_HEAD`. Pure string work, no extra process, and it makes "last fetched" genuinely per-project as intended.

options.label: Read the shared git dir's FETCH_HEAD (recommended)
options.description:
When `.git` is a file, parse `gitdir: <path>/.git/worktrees/<name>` and strip `/worktrees/<name>` to get the common dir. Read `<common>/FETCH_HEAD`. Unit-test both shapes plus the strip.

Completeness: 10/10

✅ Matches the fetch-at-root decision exactly — one fetch, one timestamp, every workroom of the project agrees, which is the behaviour the plan argued for.
✅ No extra process: the plan already parses the `gitdir:` line, so this is one more string operation on data in hand.
✅ Trivially unit-testable with a temp fixture for `.git`-as-dir, `.git`-as-file, and a malformed pointer. (human: ~1h / CC: ~5min)

options.label: Shell `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`
options.description:
Ask git for the shared dir instead of parsing paths ourselves, then read `FETCH_HEAD` from it.

Completeness: 10/10

✅ Authoritative — immune to any future change in how git lays out worktree directories, including submodules and unusual `gitdir:` forms.
✅ Reads as obviously-correct code with no path arithmetic to get subtly wrong.
❌ A third process per state read, on top of the `rev-list` D13 just added, for a path that two string operations already resolve — and process spawn is the dominant cost we measured.

options.label: Fetch inside each workroom instead
options.description:
Drop the fetch-at-root rule; run fetch in the workroom so its own `FETCH_HEAD` gets written and the per-worktree read becomes correct.

Completeness: 6/10

content.text: Locked. Two tensions left. The staleness one:

questions.question:
D16 — The counts are stale until you fetch. Is "last fetched N ago" enough? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-ov-staleness>

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. Note `TODOS.md:324` already considered automatic fetch and concluded "'just add a fetch' is the wrong shape — it needs a cadence policy and almost certainly a Settings toggle."

ELI10: Ahead/behind counts come from your local copy of what the remote looked like the last time you fetched. If a teammate pushed since then, the toolbar confidently says "5 ↑, push" when you are actually behind and the push will be rejected. The plan's answer is honesty: show "last fetched 9 minutes ago" next to the number so you can judge. But the layout ladder undercuts exactly that — the count pill is pinned to never shrink, while the "last fetched" line is the first thing abbreviated and the caption is dropped at the minimum width. So at 260pt the unverified number survives and the caveat that qualifies it is the first casualty. GitHub Desktop, the stated model, sidesteps this by fetching on its own.

Stakes if we pick wrong: a user pushes on a stale count, gets a rejection they don't understand, and the fix is a fetch the UI never suggested. Going the other way — automatic background fetching — contradicts a decision already recorded in TODOS, and turns a local read into a network call that can prompt for credentials on an unattended machine.

Recommendation: A — fetch immediately before push and pull, so the action itself is never taken on stale data, and fix the ladder so the caveat outlives the number. No background fetching, so `TODOS.md:324` stands as written and no Settings toggle is needed.

options.label: Fetch before push/pull, and fix the ladder (recommended)
options.description:
Push and pull each fetch first, then act on fresh data. Reverse the degradation priority so "last fetched" survives longer than the count pill. No background or focus-triggered fetching.

Completeness: 10/10

✅ Fixes staleness where it actually causes harm — at the moment of acting — rather than trying to keep a display continuously fresh.
✅ Free for pull, which is fetch-plus-rebase by definition, so this only adds a round trip to push.
✅ Leaves `TODOS.md:324` intact: no cadence policy, no Settings toggle, no unattended network calls.
❌ Push gets slower by one round trip, and the displayed count can still be stale between actions — it's honest, not fresh. (human: ~3h / CC: ~15min)

options.label: Auto-fetch when the inspector gains focus
options.description:
Fetch on inspector focus, guarded by an interval, so the displayed counts are usually fresh.

Completeness: 9/10

✅ The number on screen is actually trustworthy most of the time, which is what makes GitHub Desktop's equivalent readable at a glance.
✅ The visibility gating this plan already builds gives a natural, cheap trigger.
❌ Directly contradicts `TODOS.md:324`, which considered this and deferred it pending a cadence policy and a Settings toggle — and an unattended machine now makes network calls that can hit credential prompts and rate limits.

options.label: Just fix the degradation ladder
options.description:
Keep never-auto-fetch and no pre-action fetch; only reorder the ladder so the staleness caveat is not the first thing dropped.

Completeness: 6/10

✅ One-line priority change, zero behavioural risk, and it removes the specific inconsistency where the caveat vanishes before the claim it qualifies.
✅ Keeps every network call explicitly user-initiated.
❌ Push still fires on possibly-stale data, so the rejection path stays the common failure and the user has to reason about the timestamp themselves every time.

content.text: Locked B — auto-fetch on inspector focus. That knowingly supersedes `TODOS.md:324`'s deferral, so I'll update that entry rather than leave it claiming otherwise. It also raises the stakes on the last tension, because automatic network calls with a broken agent environment means silent repeated auth failures:

questions.question:
D17 — The child process can't see your SSH agent. Fix the environment? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-ov-sshenv>

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. Verified: `StatusCommandRunner.swift:50-51` builds the child env from `ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment` and overrides only `PATH`. Entitlements are NOT the problem — `project.yml:267,296-299` show hardened runtime with no App Sandbox and no entitlements file, so spawning `git` and `ssh` from the signed app is fine.

ELI10: A GUI app launched from the Dock inherits a bare environment from the system, not from your shell. The runner fixes `PATH` so `git` can be found, but nothing else. So variables your `.zshrc` sets are invisible to the child — including `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, which is how a process finds your SSH agent. Anyone using 1Password's SSH agent, gpg-agent, or a custom agent socket has that variable set in their shell and nowhere else. Their `git push` from the app cannot reach the agent, so it fails to authenticate — and the plan's error copy tells them to configure a credential helper they already have correctly configured.

Why this got worse just now: you chose auto-fetch on inspector focus. So instead of one confusing failure when they click push, these users get a silent failed fetch every time they focus the inspector.

Stakes if we pick wrong: for agent users, every network operation fails with advice that doesn't apply, and now it fails repeatedly and automatically. The app already has the machinery — `ShellEnvironment.environment()` returns the full shell-probed environment — it is just currently reserved for setup and teardown scripts.

Recommendation: A — forward the specific auth-relevant variables from the existing shell probe for network operations only, and add the missing host-key error case. Narrow, uses machinery that already exists, and doesn't change what the automatic status sweep sees.

options.label: Forward auth vars from the shell probe (recommended)
options.description:
For network ops only, merge `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `SSH_AGENT_PID`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` from `ShellEnvironment.environment()` (falling back silently when the probe failed). Add `Host key verification failed` to the classify table with its own copy.

Completeness: 10/10

✅ Makes agent-based auth work for the large population using 1Password or gpg-agent, without which auto-fetch fails silently for them forever.
✅ Reuses the existing probe rather than adding machinery, and the probe is already best-effort so a failure degrades to today's behaviour rather than breaking.
✅ Scoped to network operations, so the automatic status sweep keeps its current minimal, predictable environment.
❌ An explicit allowlist needs maintaining as new auth mechanisms appear, and the probe runs a login shell whose output is only best-effort. (human: ~3h / CC: ~15min)

options.label: Forward the whole probed environment for network ops
options.description:
Use `ShellEnvironment.environment()` wholesale for fetch/push/pull, as setup and teardown scripts already do.

Completeness: 9/10

✅ Nothing to maintain and nothing to miss — whatever the user's shell configures for git and ssh simply works, including mechanisms nobody anticipated.
✅ Consistent with how the app already runs user scripts, so there's one environment story rather than two.
❌ Hands the child every variable in the user's shell, including unrelated secrets, on a path that runs automatically now — and a `.zshrc` that sets something odd for git could change behaviour in ways that are hard to attribute.

options.label: Leave the env; improve the error copy only
options.description:
Keep `PATH`-only, but detect the agent-missing case and say so explicitly rather than blaming the credential helper.

Completeness: 5/10

✅ No environment surface change at all, so the automatic path stays fully predictable and no secret can leak into a child.
✅ At least stops giving advice that is wrong for the affected users.
❌ Their push still cannot work from inside the app no matter what the message says, so agent users are told, accurately, that the feature does not work for them — and auto-fetch keeps failing on every focus.

D19 — Which new TODOS should I file? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-todos-new>

Project/branch: workroom on `master`. Seven candidates surfaced by the outside voice that are real but out of scope for this branch. Each is described fully below; pick any subset. Anything you don't pick, I drop — I won't file it silently.

ELI10: These are problems I believe are genuine but that don't block this feature. Filing them costs nothing now and saves rediscovering them; not filing them means the reasoning dies with this session. The two I'd prioritise are the version floor (one old `git` or `jj` turns the entire feature into an unreadable raw-stderr error) and the jj sibling-workspace staleness (an action in one workroom surfaces as a mystery error in a different one, which is the hardest kind of bug to attribute).

Recommendation: file the first four. The last three are lower value — the hooks one is speculative, the bookmark accumulation is cosmetic until it isn't, and the switch duplication is pre-existing debt unrelated to this branch.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

options.label: git/jj version floor probe
options.description:
**What:** Probe `git` and `jj` versions and show a legible "needs git >= X" state instead of raw stderr.

**Why:** Verified — `git for-each-ref --format='%(bogusatom)'` fails atomically with no partial output, and the app bundles neither binary (`ShellEnvironment.path()` takes whatever is on PATH). Everything is verified against git 2.55 / jj 0.43 only; `jj bookmark` was `jj branch` before 0.18 and `tracking_*_count()` is newer still. One old tool turns the whole feature into `.other` with unreadable stderr.

**Depends on:** this feature landing. **Start:** the existing `classifyGitHubCLI` pattern (`WorkroomStatusResolver.swift:425-444`) already models "is the tool present and usable".

options.label: jj sibling-workspace staleness after rebase
options.description:
**What:** Detect and surface when a jj operation in one workroom leaves a sibling workspace stale.

**Why:** All workrooms of a jj project share one repo and op-store. `jj rebase -b @` rewrites commits; any other workspace whose `@` descends from a rewritten commit needs `jj workspace update-stale` before its next command. Today that surfaces as an unexplained error in a *different* workroom than the one the user acted in — the worst attribution problem available.

**Depends on:** pull landing. **Start:** `VCSStatusFailure.staleWorkingCopy` already exists in the taxonomy; the repair itself is a write, so it belongs to the write phase.

options.label: Gate git VCS reads, not just writes
options.description:
**What:** Route git status reads through the same per-project gate as writes.

**Why:** Verified — `WorkroomStatusResolver.resolveGit:98` never touches `self.gate`; only `resolveJJ:142` does. So D4's write gating only half-closes the contention: a fetch writing `packed-refs` while the ungated status sweep runs `git status` across N sibling worktrees reproduces exactly the `packed-refs.lock` failure the gate's own doc cites.

**Depends on:** D4 landing. **Cons:** serialising reads could slow the status sweep, so it needs measurement rather than assumption.

options.label: "New workroom from branch..." affordance
options.description:
**What:** The product-correct replacement for the branch switching cut in D14 — pick a remote or local branch and create a workroom for it.

**Why:** D14 cut switching because workrooms ARE branches, so switching one's branch makes its directory name a lie. But the underlying user need — "I want to work on that other branch" — is real, and creating a workroom is the answer the product model actually supports. Segment 1 currently routes to the existing ⌘O picker, which only lists workrooms that already exist.

**Depends on:** D14. **Start:** `OpenWorkroomDialog.swift` for the picker UI; the Go CLI's `create` already takes a branch.

options.label: Hooks + stale index.lock after a killed git
options.description:
**What:** Decide whether `post-checkout`/`post-rewrite` hooks should run from the GUI app, and probe for the `index.lock` a SIGKILLed git leaves behind.

**Why:** Reasoning-only. Hooks are arbitrary user scripts, now running with the launchd environment and subject to SIGTERM at timeout plus `ProcessTree.killTree` at +2s (`StatusCommandRunner.swift:88-98`). A hook that runs a package manager gets killed at 120s. The plan probes for `rebase-merge` after a timed-out pull but never for `index.lock`, which would break every subsequent read for that workroom.

**Depends on:** pull landing.

options.label: jj push-<id> bookmark accumulation
options.description:
**What:** Prune or hide the `push-<changeid>` bookmarks that jj's anonymous-push path mints.

**Why:** Every push of an unbookmarked `@` creates a permanent tracked `push-<id>` bookmark. Over weeks these accumulate with no cleanup. Also an unresolved asymmetry: git is "never `--force`", but re-pushing an amended change via `--change` moves the bookmark non-fast-forward by design.

**Depends on:** push landing. Lower priority now that D14 cut the picker, since there is no branch list surfacing them yet.

options.label: DiffModeSwitch / MarkdownModeSwitch duplication
options.description:
**What:** Collapse two near-identical 2-segment switch controls into one generic control.

**Why:** Pre-existing, unrelated to this branch. `TerminalTabStrip.swift:725-767` and `:769-815` are a literal copy of each other differing only in which two-way choice they present. Flagged under see-something-say-something since I read them while looking for a segmented-control precedent.

**Depends on:** nothing. Pure cleanup.
